node.label: R. Bin Wong
node.date_label: with Will, Nourish the People 1991 · China Transformed 1997 · with Rosenthal, Before and Beyond Divergence 2011 · “Divergence Displaced” 2016
node.description: A historian of China at UCLA whose China Transformed (1997) compared Chinese and European economic change, state formation and popular protest without treating Europe as the norm. As Joel Mokyr read it, Wong held that before 1800 Europe and China shared “Smithian expansion, rural industry, population expansion, a growth in consumer demand”, and that the “supply-driven Industrial Revolution that followed the demand-led Industrious Revolution in Europe did not happen in China” (1997, p. 31, as Mokyr quotes it). Kenneth Pomeranz wrote that he was “following a procedure outlined in Wong’s recent China Transformed”, while giving “greater stress than Wong does on global conjunctures” (2000). Wong later said that the book had located Europe’s difference in science and technology, “following arguments of E. A. Wrigley” on coal (2016). With Jean-Laurent Rosenthal, in Before and Beyond Divergence (2011), he turned to “political fragmentation in Europe and the presence of an unitary state for the Chinese empire”: war drew European craft production into cities, so that the question became “why was industrialization more likely to occur in Western Europe than in China” (his 2016 account); as Debin Ma reported the mechanism, higher urban wages there biased innovation towards saving labour. Ma judged the book “a good contribution in the Great Divergence debate” but found this “stimulating and striking hypothesis” “supported by fairly meager evidence in the chapter” (2012). In “Divergence Displaced” (2016) he judged Brenner’s agrarian social relations, Pomeranz’s coal and colonies and his own earlier book alike open to “non-falsifiability”. Mokyr had objected that “Bin Wong does not cite any book by Needham” (2002 draft).
node.representative_figures_and_works: R. Bin Wong; with Pierre-Étienne Will, Nourish the People: The State Civilian Granary System in China, 1650–1850 (1991); China Transformed: Historical Change and the Limits of European Experience (1997); with Jean-Laurent Rosenthal, Before and Beyond Divergence: The Politics of Economic Change in China and Europe (2011); “Divergence Displaced: Patterns of Economic and Political Change in Early Modern and Modern Global History” (Comparativ, 2016). Readers: Kenneth Pomeranz (2000); Joel Mokyr (2002); Philip Huang (2002); Prasannan Parthasarathi (2011); Debin Ma (2012); Morgan Kelly, Joel Mokyr and Cormac Ó Gráda (2014).
node.scope_note: Read in his own words on 2026-10-18: “Divergence Displaced” (Comparativ, 2016, open access), pp. 71–80 closely, with pp. 81–100, a critique of Peer Vries, skimmed; China Transformed only in chapter openings read in an earlier revision. China Transformed’s argument is otherwise given through Mokyr’s quotations (2002), Pomeranz (2000), Huang (2002) and Parthasarathi (2011); Before and Beyond Divergence (2011, with Rosenthal) through Wong’s own 2016 summary and Ma’s review (2012); Nourish the People (1991, with Will) is dated from metadata only. Co-authored arguments are his co-authors’ as well. His statement that China Transformed followed Wrigley is a 2016 retrospective. The “California School” is a readers’ label, attributed by Frank and Vries to Goldstone, and is not used here as Wong’s own. The Great Divergence debate is held by capitalismdebates; global/comparison, global/eurasian_states and global/reciprocal_comparison_resources keep his comparative method.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reciprocal comparison of China’s and Europe’s advanced regions: Pomeranz followed “a procedure outlined in Wong’s recent China Transformed”, with “greater stress than Wong does on global conjunctures” (2000)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Pomeranz’s own words, The Great Divergence (2000, pp. 7–8, later-edition preview, read): a regional approach “anticipated in important ways by my colleague R. Bin Wong” (p. 7); “Here, too, I am following a procedure outlined in Wong’s recent China Transformed … viewing both sides of the comparison as ‘deviations’ when seen through the expectations of the other, rather than leaving one as always the norm” (p. 8); “my concrete application of this reciprocal comparative method has some significant differences from Wong’s”, with “greater stress than Wong does on global conjunctures and reciprocal influences” (p. 8 and n. 13). Readers: Parthasarathi (2011, p. 5): “Kenneth Pomeranz builds upon this work”; Huang (2002, p. 520) traces Pomeranz’s use of the industrious revolution to “R. Bin Wong’s brief discussion earlier (1997, 30–31)”. Wong (Comparativ 2016, read): Pomeranz rejected “numerous putative differences … including my China Transformed” (p. 73); China Transformed “followed the same method” (p. 76); both books “shared … the basic problem of non-falsifiability” (p. 77). The same debt is recorded as the strand global/reciprocal_comparison_resources (carried by edge_898); this arrow makes it a relationship between the two entries.

proposed_edges.relationship: From the limits of European experience to political scale: with Rosenthal, Wong argued that European fragmentation and warfare concentrated manufacturing in cities, where higher wage costs favoured labour-saving techniques (2011, as Wong summarised in 2016 and Ma reported in 2012); in 2016 he recast divergence from “why Britain” to a more general transformation
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own words, “Divergence Displaced” (Comparativ 26:3, 2016, pp. 77–78, read): “Rosenthal and I ended up focusing on an important political difference between China and Europe – political fragmentation in Europe and the presence of an unitary state for the Chinese empire”; war gave “craft producers an incentive to locate in cities”; “We turned the issue of divergence from a question of why was Britain the first industrializer to why was industrialization more likely to occur in Western Europe than in China” (p. 77); “By making the question of the great divergence a more general one we recognize that even a profoundly transformative process like modern economic growth could take place in several ways and begin at several locations” (p. 78). Before and Beyond Divergence (2011) is unread; Ma’s review (EH.Net 2012, read in full in revision 1.145) reports the same dichotomy of “a unified and centralized imperial China versus a politically fragmented Europe” and the mechanism: warfare brought “a greater degree of concentration of trade and manufacturing in urban locations”, and, “With higher urban wages”, innovation in Europe “would be more biased towards saving labor than in China”. Ma finds this “stimulating and striking hypothesis” “supported by fairly meager evidence in the chapter”, and the evidence on public goods “even shakier”. He also reports the authors’ challenge to “the accepted thesis of China being a high interest rate and capital scarce country”, and judges the book “a good contribution in the Great Divergence debate” for addressing “some of the key issues beyond what has been done recently by Pomeranz, Allen and others”, though “far less so when it comes to providing credible support for its own thesis”. The wage mechanism is Ma’s report; Wong’s 2016 summary gives the move of craft production to cities. Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda (2014, p. 16.2) say Rosenthal and Wong “adopted” Allen’s induced-innovation argument “wholesale”. China Transformed (1997), as Mokyr quotes it, held that the “supply-driven Industrial Revolution that followed the demand-led Industrious Revolution in Europe did not happen in China” (p. 31); Mokyr objected that “Bin Wong does not cite any book by Needham” (2002 draft, pp. 3–4). The co-authored argument is Rosenthal’s as well as Wong’s.

proposed_edges.relationship: Brenner’s agrarian social relations, like Pomeranz’s coal and colonies, are traits particular to Britain, so that their necessity “cannot be falsified” (2016)
proposed_edges.map_label: Wong questions the falsifiability of Brenner’s explanation, 2016
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Wong, “Divergence Displaced” (Comparativ 2016, pp. 74–75, read): “when my colleague and Marxist historian Robert Brenner famously argues that it is the absence of the agrarian social relations found in Britain that prevented the emergence of capitalism elsewhere, the importance of the system through which he sees the modern world economy emerging cannot be falsified because the enclosures and the social relations that attended them were particular to Britain. Like Pomeranz’s coal and colonies, Brenner cites traits that are British and not present elsewhere” (p. 74); “Neither the scientific revolution nor agrarian social relations lend themselves very easily to counterfactual exercises because they are themselves so large and encompassing” (p. 75). He allows that such traits “could in fact be factors helping to explain the industrial revolution” (p. 75). A methodological critique in one passage, citing the Aston and Philpin collection; it does not dispute Brenner’s evidence. Brenner’s other respondents are on capitalismdebates → robert_brenner (edge_1078), which does not name Wong.
